notes: I will start with the physics motivation and detector requirements, then introduce the simulation and reconstruction framework. I will then present our study of 3 production mechanisms with a positron beam. My focus is on the experimental work: simulating rare backgrounds efficiently, selecting signal events, and estimating the sensitivity. I will explain the theory assumptions where we need them.

title: Physics Motivation and DarkSHINE Experiment
body:
01 / DISSERTATION PRE-DEFENCE

Physics Motivation and
DarkSHINE Experiment

Light dark matter and an accelerator-based missing-energy search
notes: Gravitational observations give us evidence for dark matter. To search for it in the laboratory, we need a model of how it interacts with ordinary matter.

title: Evidence for dark matter
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Evidence for dark matter

Extended mass distributions

Orbital velocities remain high beyond the luminous disc.

Mass and gas separate

Lensing traces gravitating matter beyond the hot gas.

A non-baryonic component

The matter budget is constrained across cosmic scales.

These observations constrain the abundance and distribution of dark matter; its particle identity remains unknown.
Clowe et al., ApJ 648 (2006) L109; Planck 2018.
notes: We see evidence for dark matter over a wide range of scales, from galaxy rotation curves to cluster lensing and the cosmic microwave background. In merging clusters, the hot gas and the mass inferred from lensing can be spatially separated. Together, these observations give us information about the abundance and distribution of dark matter. Its particle identity and its coupling to ordinary matter remain unknown.
source: Clowe et al., ApJ 648 (2006) L109; Planck 2018. Image: supplied reference assets.

title: What observations constrain
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# What observations constrain

Observational requirements

Long-lived on cosmological time scales.

Sufficiently cold to form the observed structures.

Model-dependent bounds

Statistics, thermal history and late energy injection determine the relevant limits.
notes: The observations constrain different properties of dark matter. Its lifetime has to be long enough for it to survive until today, and its motion in the early Universe has to be consistent with the small-scale structure we observe. The phase-space bound applies to fermions. Thermal free-streaming bounds depend on the assumed early velocity distribution. BBN (Big Bang Nucleosynthesis) and the CMB (Cosmic Microwave Background) constrain new species in thermal contact with the Standard Model, as well as later energy injection. These constraints motivate searches for light dark matter, but they rely on different assumptions and do not give a single lower mass limit for every model. For this study, we use a vector-portal benchmark in the MeV to GeV range.

title: Complementary dark-matter searches
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Complementary dark-matter searches
DarkSHINE probes controlled production through missing energy and momentum.
notes: Direct detection looks for interactions of Galactic dark matter in a detector. It becomes difficult when the recoil energy is very small. Indirect detection looks for products of dark-matter annihilation or decay. At an accelerator, we try to produce dark matter in a controlled collision. We know the beam energy, so we can search for events with less visible energy than expected. This search does not depend on the local halo density. Relating the result to the cosmic abundance still requires a dark-sector model. The experimental challenge is to reject ordinary interactions in which visible particles escape detection.

body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# The dark photon as a vector portal

notes:
This equation describes kinetic mixing between the photon and the dark photon. The parameter epsilon gives the dark photon a small coupling to the electromagnetic current. Its mass determines the kinematics, and epsilon squared approximately scales the production rate. We assume that the dark photon can decay to lighter dark-sector particles, with an invisible branching fraction close to 1. I therefore show the projected limits as a function of mediator mass and kinetic mixing. Later, when comparing with thermal relic targets, I will specify the dark coupling and the mass ratio. We do not need to choose a detailed ultraviolet model for this detector study.

8 GeVDesign beam energy

EOT: electrons on target.

notes: SHINE stands for Shanghai High Repetition-Rate XFEL and Extreme Light Facility. We take an electron-beam design energy of 8 GeV and a design repetition rate of 1 MHz as inputs to the DarkSHINE conceptual design. The electron programme uses a dedicated extraction branch alongside the free-electron-laser beamlines. The benchmark count is three times ten to the fourteen incident electrons, expressed as EOT, or electrons on target. These are the design parameters and beam count used for the simulation study. Positron delivery is a proposed extension of this electron programme.

title: DarkSHINE detector conceptual design Baseline 1
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# DarkSHINE detector conceptual design Baseline 1
notes:
This is the DarkSHINE detector conceptual design in the Baseline 1 configuration. Baseline 1 uses a non-staggered twenty by twenty by eleven LYSO ECAL and the original uniform-absorber HCAL. It is the common detector benchmark for the electron and positron sensitivity studies. The Baseline Design Report documents the experiment and detector studies.

Following the beam, the tagging tracker measures the incident electron momentum in the magnetic field. The electron crosses a thin tungsten target, and the recoil tracker measures the outgoing charged particle. The ECAL measures electromagnetic energy and its spatial distribution. The larger HCAL detects hadrons and penetrating muons so that we can reject their visible activity. The trackers use silicon strips, while the ECAL is a segmented crystal array.

Click sequence: Tracking, ECAL, HCAL.

title: Detector requirements for a missing-energy search
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Detector requirements for a missing-energy search
SubsystemRequirement / benchmark
Tagging trackerHit resolution ; momentum resolution at 8 GeV
Tungsten target; limit multiple scattering
Recoil trackerAccept recoils from to 2 GeV; hit resolution
LYSO ECALHigh granularity; precise e/γ energy measurement
Fe/scintillator HCALNeutron veto inefficiency for ; at lower energies
notes: The Baseline 1 requirements follow from the missing-energy measurement. The tagging tracker needs a hit precision below 10 micrometres and a momentum resolution below 2 percent at 8 GeV. The tungsten target is 0.1 radiation lengths thick to limit multiple scattering. The recoil tracker measures soft charged particles, with the quoted acceptance extending from about 30 MeV to 2 GeV. The ECAL needs high granularity and precise energy measurement to identify localised electromagnetic deposits and events with low visible energy. The HCAL requirements are driven by the neutron background: veto inefficiency below ten to the minus five above roughly 2 GeV, and below ten to the minus three at lower energies. The ECAL and HCAL design papers are collaborative research contributions supporting these subsystem studies.

title: Electron-mode signal and background rejection
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Electron-mode signal and background rejection
SignalElectron beam

One soft recoil electron with substantial missing energy and momentum.

SelectionVisible vetoes

Measurements used together

  • Exactly one incident particle
  • A recoil carrying less momentum
  • Low electromagnetic energy
  • No significant hadronic or muon activity

Hard bremsstrahlung is abundant. Rare photonuclear, electronuclear and muon-pair processes can leave poorly measured energy.

The sensitivity is controlled by the rare surviving tails of Standard Model interactions.
notes:
In electron mode, dark bremsstrahlung produces a dark photon that decays invisibly, together with a recoil electron. The recoil electron usually carries only part of the beam energy. Ordinary bremsstrahlung can also leave a soft electron, but the photon normally deposits its energy in the ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter). The cases of concern are rare processes that transfer this energy to hadrons or muons, or send it outside the detector acceptance. We use the measured momentum, electromagnetic energy and HCAL (Hadronic Calorimeter) veto together to reject these events. The simulation needs to describe both the usual electromagnetic response and the rare shower tails that pass the cuts.

Presenter cue: Start with the signal diagram. Click once to introduce the combined detector requirements and backgrounds.
source: J. Chen et al., Sci. China Phys. Mech. Astron. 66, 211062 (2023).

title: Standard Model background hierarchy
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Standard Model background hierarchy

Hard-photon branches

: identified by tracker and ECAL.

Photonuclear / : hadrons and muons.

Different rejection mechanisms

Electronuclear produces hadrons. HCAL vetoes hadronic and muonic activity.

Residual background

Muon pairs are effectively rejected by HCAL. PN / EN tails require extrapolation into the signal region.

J. Chen et al., Sci. China Phys. Mech. Astron. 66, 211062 (2023); Baseline Design Report, arXiv:2411.09345.
notes:
Most beam electrons pass through the thin target. Hard bremsstrahlung produces a recoil electron and an energetic photon. Electron–positron conversion is frequent, and tracking and the ECAL can identify those particles. The rarer photonuclear and muon-pair branches put energy into hadrons or muons, making the HCAL veto essential. Electronuclear reactions provide another hadronic source.

After applying the veto, the paper finds muon pairs effectively rejected by HCAL. PN and EN require residual-background estimates in the signal region. This is where the low-energy tails matter and inclusive statistics become insufficient. We therefore simulate six dedicated samples: PN, EN and muon-pair production, each in the target and ECAL, alongside 2.5 billion inclusive events. The rare-process samples are normalised by their branching ratios and used to study rejection and extrapolate the nuclear-background tails. This motivates a framework that can populate and inspect these rare sub-processes efficiently.
source: J. Chen et al., Sci. China Phys. Mech. Astron. 66, 211062 (2023), Secs. 4.2, 5 and 6.1; Fig. 8 and Table 2.

title: The DarkSHINE software framework
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# The DarkSHINE software framework
From a beam particle to an analysis sample
8 GeV e⁻ beam
My contributions: General design of software framework, DSimu, DEvent, rare-process biasing and filtering, and ACTS integration.
notes:
The framework connects the incident beam to a physics prediction. DSimu generates particles and simulates their detector interactions. DEvent carries the truth and hit collections. DAna runs digitisation, reconstruction and analysis, and DDis lets us inspect individual events.

The four plots on the right are physical outputs from the CDR electron-mode simulation. The coloured curves correspond to different dark-photon masses. The dark distributions in the energy, transverse-momentum and angle panels show the inclusive background. The recoil-energy plot separates the softer signal electrons from the background concentrated near the beam energy. The transverse-momentum plot gives a complementary discriminant; this panel requires recoil energy between 50 MeV and 4 GeV. Larger recoil angles and the transverse separation at the detector surface connect these kinematics to the tracker acceptance. The separation panel shows the signal mass dependence. These are the observables we need the framework to produce for detector design and event selection.

I contributed to the general framework design and developed the simulation software, DSimu, the event data structure, DEvent, rare-process biasing and filtering, and ACTS integration. I will now explain how we made large simulation samples more practical to produce and store.
source: DSS software framework; X. Zhu, Nucl. Part. Phys. Proc. 346 (2024) 57.

title: A common event model: DEvent
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# A common event model: DEvent
What a stored event lets us study
Truth particles + stepsMomentum, energy, origin, endpoint and ancestryTrace the interaction that produced a background
Simulated hitsDeposited energy, position, time and cell IDStudy shower topology and detector response
Response + reconstructed objectsCell signals, fitted tracks and clustersBuild visible energy, recoil momentum and vetoes
One event, linked views

Follow the particle history into detector deposits, then compare with reconstructed tracks and calorimeter response.
notes: DEvent carries several views of the same physical event. Truth particles and steps tell us the momenta, energies, origins and interaction history. Simulated hits record deposited energy, positions, times and detector cell identifiers. Detector-response collections and reconstructed objects then provide cell signals, fitted tracks and clusters. The event display on the right shows why the associations matter: we can follow a particle into a shower and ask which deposits it produced. For a background that enters the signal region, we can trace its origin, inspect the veto activity and check whether reconstruction missed a track or cluster. Named collections also let us rerun response or reconstruction algorithms from stored Geant4 particle and hit records. We choose the persisted collections according to the study that needs them.

title: Geometry navigation and event-record optimisation
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Geometry navigation and event-record optimisation
Store the quantities needed for physics

Smaller records, explicit content

InformationStored quantities / change
Particle kinematicspₓ, pᵧ, p_z, E, m → float
Origin and trajectoryVertex and endpoint x, y, z → float
Detector hitsEnergy, time, x, y, z → float; compact cell IDs
Remove duplicationCalculate |p| from components; identify particles by PDG ID
Step historyRecord primary-electron steps in the tracker region
60.1 → 13.7 KB/eventEvent-record benchmark
Navigate a finely segmented detector

Bounding volume hierarchy

Nested bounding volumes reduce volume checks at each Geant4 step.

260 → 42 ms/eventNavigation benchmark
notes: After obtaining these physics outputs, we optimised the software for large event production. The changes target event records and Geant4 geometry navigation. The storage optimisation starts from the physics information we need. Particle records store momentum components, energy, mass, production vertices and endpoints. Hits store deposited energy, time, position and detector or cell identifiers. These floating-point fields use float rather than double. We also remove duplicated quantities: the momentum magnitude can be calculated from its components, and the PDG identifier replaces a repeated particle-name string. The historical optimisation restricted step histories to the initial electron in the tracker region, where its trajectory is needed. Together with record and memory-layout changes, the reported event size falls from 60.1 to as little as 13.7 kilobytes. Separately, a bounding volume hierarchy speeds navigation through the segmented detector. It reduces the number of individual volumes Geant4 has to test; the benchmark falls from 260 to 42 milliseconds per event. The two numbers describe different optimisations and configurations.

title: Generator-level filtering with staged Geant4 tracking
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Generator-level filtering with staged Geant4 tracking
Primary interaction

Was enough energy transferred?

Check the primary energy loss and, when requested, a hard bremsstrahlung photon.

Rare secondary process

Did the required interaction occur?

Select process or particle type, longitudinal region and energy interval.

Visible shower energy

Can this event still pass?

Stop once accumulated truth ECAL energy exceeds the production bound.
notes: The filter is organised around the physics of rare backgrounds. At stage zero, we run Geant4 tracking for the primary particle and defer its secondaries. We can inspect the primary energy loss and require a hard bremsstrahlung photon. At stage one, we release secondaries from the chosen longitudinal region. A process filter can require a photonuclear, electronuclear or muon-pair interaction and an energy transfer in the parent step. A particle filter instead checks the secondary species and its energy. Only when the requested conditions are met do we release the remaining tracks. There is also an early ECAL veto: once the accumulated deposited energy exceeds the production upper bound, subsequent shower development cannot reduce that accumulated energy. These decisions use Geant4 particle and energy-deposit information and define the generated sample. Reconstructed momentum and calibrated calorimeter selections are applied later.

title: Generator-level filter performance
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Generator-level filter performance
8 GeV electron sample
ECAL-energy selection
0.11%

Pass in the prefiltered sample with a reconstructed recoil track.

Missing-momentum threshold migration
6 / EOT

Cross the 4 GeV threshold after reconstruction and also pass the truth ECAL-energy cut.

About five orders of magnitude fewer stored event records at the same simulated EOT.
notes: The main gain from this filter is at the storage stage. In the inclusive production test, we saved 270,310 events from twenty billion incident electrons. The filter efficiency, defined here as the fraction of beam events saved, is 0.0014 percent. We therefore write about 74,000 times fewer event records at the same simulated EOT: a storage-efficiency improvement of roughly five orders of magnitude. This makes background production at high EOT practical to store and analyse. The two plots show the physics behind the selection. On the left, only 0.11 percent of the prefiltered sample with a reconstructed recoil track has ECAL energy below 4 GeV. On the right, the blue histogram contains events with one reconstructed recoil track and reconstructed missing momentum above 4 GeV, plotted against truth missing momentum. Adding truth ECAL energy below 4 GeV leaves only six threshold-migration events in twenty million incident electrons. These distributions guide the production cuts. Next, rare-process biasing provides the statistics needed for specific background final states.
source: inclusive_filter.key, slides 2 and 5; supplied generator_filter_tracker_missing_p_cut.png and generator_filter_ecal_cut.png. Statistical denominators confirmed by Xuliang Zhu.

title: Rare-process biasing and physical normalisation
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Rare-process biasing and physical normalisation
01 | Enrich the physics of interest

Choose process, material and energy

  • PN, EN or muon-pair production in the target / ECAL
  • Increase the selected interaction cross section above an energy threshold
  • Simulate secondary interactions, energy deposits and leakage
02 | Measure the rate dependence on bias
Eligible beam events × physical interaction probability
Enrich rare final states for detector studies; recover their rate from the production normalisation.
notes:
Biasing lets us study final states that are too rare to populate efficiently in inclusive simulation. We choose the interaction, the material region and an energy threshold, then enhance that interaction cross section. Geant4 then tracks the secondary particles and simulates their interactions, so we can study hadronic activity, muon tracks and leakage. Click once to show a muon-pair conversion scan in the ECAL. The interaction probability increases with the bias factor and eventually saturates. We fit this dependence and evaluate the physical probability at bias factor one. Multiplying by the fraction of incident events with an eligible particle gives the process rate per beam particle. This gives the expected rare-process event count for a specified EOT or POT. The positron analysis uses its dedicated process-rate normalisations.

Presenter cue: Explain which rare final states are enriched, then click once to connect sampling to the physical rate.

title: Parallel event simulation
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Parallel event simulation
Independent beam events

One physics chain per worker

Each worker runs generation, particle tracking in Geant4 and event filling with its own random and event state.

Particles + ancestryTracker hitsECAL / HCAL deposits

Merge the same named collections for reconstruction and analysis.

10⁶ events, eight concurrent units:
8-thread job: 15,328 s
8 single-thread jobs: 16,648 s
notes: Beam events are independent, so the natural unit of parallel work is a complete event. Each worker generates the primary, simulates its particle trajectories and interactions with Geant4 and fills its particle and detector-hit collections. Implementing this required worker-local event storage, random-number handling and changes to shared framework state. The output still uses the same collections, so the downstream reconstruction and analysis can read the merged sample. The chart shows the measured throughput as the worker count changes. In the eight-unit benchmark, one eight-thread job takes 15,328 seconds, compared with 16,648 seconds for eight single-thread jobs. The practical gain is larger production samples through a shared physics interface. The historical development also reported inclusive-process checks.

title: Optical response with a lookup table
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Optical response with a lookup table
Replace repeated photon propagation

Predict detected light and arrival time

Tabulate response versus emission position and direction.

Detection probabilityPhoton transit time

Sample this response for scintillation photons during shower simulation.

~200 → ~4 s/eventFull optical tracking → LUT

Collected light versus emission depth and angle.

Arrival-time response of the detected photons.

Validate the light yield and time response; the tested detection efficiencies agree within 5%.
Credit: Qibin Liu
notes: The LUT replaces repeated optical-photon propagation with a detector-response model. It is indexed by the photon emission position and direction. We need two outputs: the detection probability, which controls the collected light, and the transit-time distribution, which controls when it reaches the sensor. The middle plot compares the LUT detection efficiency with full optical-photon tracking over depth and angle; the difference stays within five percent in the tested configuration. The right plot compares the transit-time spectra. Most populated bins lie near one, while late photons have larger statistical uncertainty. In the complete-event benchmark, this reduces the time from about 200 seconds to four seconds. This optical-response work is Qibin Liu's collaboration contribution, integrated into the framework.

title: Digitisation connects deposits to observables
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Digitisation connects deposits to observables
Physics response model

From photons to cell energy

SiPM saturation and recovery, electronic noise, finite dynamic range and ADC sampling.

Pulse amplitude / integralCell energyTiming

Cell energies feed the ECAL total-energy and maximum-cell selections.

Credit: Qibin Liu
notes: Digitisation converts simulated deposits into measurable signals. After scintillation and light collection, each detected photon contributes a single-photoelectron pulse, shown in the middle. The time sum of those pulses forms the cell waveform on the right. The model includes SiPM saturation and recovery, electronic noise, the available dynamic range and ADC sampling. Calibration then converts the chosen response estimator into cell energy. This matters directly for our analysis: summing the cell energies gives the visible ECAL energy, while the largest cell response defines the maximum-cell observable. The configuration records which optical or parameterised response produced those quantities. These studies are Qibin Liu's collaboration contribution.

title: Track finding and fitting
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Track finding and fitting
From strip measurements to a momentum estimate
01 | Find the track

Associate hits across layers; rank circle candidates and remove accepted hits.

02 | Fit the trajectory

Propagate through the field and material with measurement errors, energy loss and multiple scattering.

03 | Evaluate tracking performance

Momentum resolution versus beam energy and layer count constrains the recoil measurement.

DarkSHINE Collaboration, Baseline Design Report, arXiv:2411.09345
notes:
Track finding identifies which strip measurements belong to a common trajectory. The legacy finder ranks circle candidates and removes accepted hits before continuing. Track fitting estimates momentum and covariance while accounting for the magnetic field, material, measurement errors, energy loss and multiple scattering.

The CDR plot shows the recoil tracker's relative momentum resolution as a function of beam energy, for four to ten tracker layers. It is a detector-performance study. At low energies, multiple scattering affects the measurement; at high energies, the small curvature and available lever arm limit the resolution. Six layers provide the Baseline 1 balance between tracking information and material. The reconstructed momentum and track multiplicity then enter the missing-momentum selection. The framework also supports the GenFit and Riemann fitting implementations described in the software study.
source: DarkSHINE Baseline Design Report, arXiv:2411.09345; CDR TrackerMomentumReso.pdf.

title: ACTS integration in DarkSHINE
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# ACTS integration in DarkSHINE
Reconstruction interfaces
Example output: track-parameter pull
Fit residual relative to its estimated uncertainty
ACTS provides fitted states and covariance, vertex candidates, and track extrapolation to ECAL.
My contributions: ACTS sequencer, geometry/field adapters and reconstruction interfaces.
notes: ACTS needs the detector information in its own tracking representation. We convert the geometry into surfaces and strip-pair hits into measurements and source links, with consistent coordinates for the field and momentum. The reference sequencer then uses truth-smeared seeds, combinatorial Kalman finding, trajectory conversion and vertex reconstruction. Its outputs include fitted states and covariance, track quality information and impact states extrapolated to the ECAL. The plot is an earlier truth-assisted fitter integration test. It shows a track-parameter pull versus transverse momentum: the fitted-minus-truth residual divided by its estimated uncertainty. This illustrates how the integration produces a physical performance diagnostic, alongside the track objects needed by the analysis. My contributions are the sequencer and geometry, field and reconstruction interfaces. The later ACTS developments are separate from the frozen reconstruction used in the positron study.
source: Candidate contribution: ACTS sequencer, geometry/field adapters and reconstruction interfaces.

title: Positron-Beam-Mode Analysis
body:
03 / DISSERTATION PRE-DEFENCE

Positron-Beam-Mode
Analysis

Three production mechanisms, three exclusive reconstructed categories
notes: I will now use this simulation chain to study positron running. I will start with the additional production mechanisms and then follow them through the detector selection. We keep the baseline 1 detector so that we can compare with the published electron-beam projection using the same detector design.

title: Why a positron beam?
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Why a positron beam?
for an 8 GeV beam and an electron initially at rest.
notes:
A positron can undergo nuclear bremsstrahlung, just like an electron, and it can also annihilate with an atomic electron. Non-resonant annihilation produces a photon and a dark photon. In resonant annihilation, the electron and positron produce a dark photon that decays to a dark-matter pair, with no accompanying hard visible particle. For an electron initially at rest, an 8 GeV positron gives a centre-of-mass energy of about 90 MeV. This provides a mass scale that we do not have in the electron bremsstrahlung channel. To find the sensitivity gain, we also need to account for the visible final state, detector efficiency, migration between selections and positron backgrounds. I will compare the production rates and detector-level selections for these 3 mechanisms.

Presenter cue: Click 0: introduce dark bremsstrahlung, which also occurs with an electron beam. Click 1: introduce non-resonant and resonant annihilation together, then explain the 90.4 MeV scale.

title: Production mechanisms at 8 GeV
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Production mechanisms at 8 GeV
Annihilation kinematics

Annihilation adds a mass scale

For an electron at rest,

Bound-electron motion broadens the annihilation kinematics.

The radiative endpoint and resonant enhancement motivate a detector-level comparison near 90 MeV.
X. Zhu et al., arXiv:2609.05900.
notes: Nuclear bremsstrahlung covers a broad range of mediator masses. Non-resonant annihilation is limited by the available centre-of-mass energy, and resonant production is enhanced near that energy. An 8 GeV positron annihilating with an electron at rest has a centre-of-mass energy of 90.4 MeV. Bound electrons are moving, which broadens this picture and allows the resonant samples to extend above the stationary-electron value. We generate on-shell mediators in this study. We do not include a separate off-shell dark-matter-pair calculation. We then apply the detector selection to find the accepted yield for each mechanism.
source: X. Zhu et al., arXiv:2609.05900. Original cross-section plot.

title: Signal and background samples
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Signal and background samples
Efficiency samples

Signal grid

MechanismMass points
Dark bremsstrahlung30
Non-resonant annihilation18
Resonant annihilation23

events per channel–mass point.

CalcHEP kinematics followed by Geant4 detector simulation.

Background predictions

Background production

  • PN, EN and muon-pair conversion
  • Target/tracker and ECAL locations
  • Additional target-annihilation sample
  • Independent inclusive sample: POT

Common benchmark: 8 GeV, POT, baseline 1 detector.

Equal generated signal counts measure efficiency. Cross sections determine the physical mixture.
arXiv:2609.05900
notes: We simulate 30 bremsstrahlung mass points, 18 non-resonant points and 23 resonant points, with 100,000 events at each point. We calculate efficiencies from these equal-sized samples and apply the physical rates afterwards. For backgrounds, we generate dedicated biased samples of photonuclear, positron-nuclear and muon-pair processes. Production in the target or tracker is separate from production in the ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter). We use the EN (Electronuclear) label for the positron-nuclear sample in this campaign. We also generate ordinary annihilation in the target. POT denotes positrons on target. An independent inclusive sample contains the equivalent of 2.5 × 10⁹ incident positrons. We use it to check the dedicated predictions without adding it to the background total. All sensitivity results use baseline 1.

Tagging tracks= 1= 1= 1

Missing momentum> 4 GeV——

Track multiplicity separates SR1. Complementary ECAL maximum-cell cuts separate SR2 and SR3.
notes: We assign events to reconstructed categories without using the generated process label. Every category requires exactly 1 tagging track. SR1 (Signal Region 1) requires 1 recoil track and missing momentum above 4 GeV. SR2 (Signal Region 2) and SR3 (Signal Region 3) require 0 recoil tracks and total ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter) energy below 2 GeV. We divide these samples at a maximum-cell energy of 1 MeV, with events on the boundary assigned to region 2. Every region also requires low total HCAL (Hadronic Calorimeter) energy and no cell above 1 MeV. The selections do not overlap. Events with additional tracks or a failed veto are rejected.

title: Momentum and total-energy discrimination
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Momentum and total-energy discrimination
The production filter requires missing momentum > 1 GeV. The final SR1 requirement is > 4 GeV.
arXiv:2609.05900
notes: On the left is missing momentum. The background sample already passes the loose production filter at 1 GeV; the final analysis cut is 4 GeV. On the right is the total ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter) energy for non-resonant annihilation. Near the mediator-mass endpoint, the accompanying photon is soft. The 90 MeV signal can therefore pass a low-energy cut even though a photon is produced. The detector response and acceptance determine the fraction that passes.

title: Maximum-cell energy separates the zero-track sample
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Maximum-cell energy separates the zero-track sample
defines SR2; defines SR3.
notes: For events with no recoil track, the largest ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter) cell helps distinguish a photon deposit from a nearly empty calorimeter. The non-resonant distribution changes with mediator mass because the photon kinematics change. Resonant annihilation usually leaves little activity, although interactions in the tracker material can produce deposits. We also cut on total energy because many small deposits can add up. The 1 MeV values are selection thresholds in the benchmark detector-response model.

All nine channel-to-region efficiencies enter the signal prediction.
notes: These curves show the cutflow efficiency for each production mechanism in its primary region. Each curve is normalised to the generated sample. We apply the cross sections later to obtain the expected mixture of processes. The backups contain all 9 channel-to-region efficiency curves. An event can enter a different region if its recoil track is not reconstructed, or if its photon escapes detection or falls below threshold. For example, bremsstrahlung can enter the regions with no recoil track. Its efficiency in the low-activity region becomes substantial toward the upper end of the mass grid. We include these migrations when predicting the signal. The next slide gives the expected yields at 90 MeV.

title: Background rejection in the available simulation

# Background rejection in the available simulation
PN ECAL | cumulative unweighted simulated counts
No simulated events survive the full selection; the residual background is estimated by extrapolation.
notes: This cutflow follows photonuclear interactions in the ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter). The recoil-track cut first divides events into categories with 1 or 0 recoil tracks. The next cut uses momentum in SR1 (Signal Region 1), the maximum-cell lower bound in SR2 (Signal Region 2) and total electromagnetic energy in SR3 (Signal Region 3). The HCAL (Hadronic Calorimeter) veto reduces the samples further, and the final electromagnetic-energy cut removes the remaining simulated events. These bars are unweighted simulation counts, before scaling to the 3 × 10¹⁴ POT benchmark. No event in the inclusive or dedicated samples passes a complete region selection. Because the samples are finite, this does not imply that the physical background is 0.

Rate validation

Independent comparison

The inclusive sample tests the populated survival trend.

notes: We normalise each dedicated sample to its equivalent unbiased POT using the number of generation attempts, generator acceptance and physical branching ratio. The number of attempts differs from the number of stored events, so we keep track of both. We then compare the sum of the dedicated samples, including target annihilation, with the independent inclusive sample where enough events are available. This comparison checks the normalisation and shapes in the populated sidebands. The dedicated samples provide the residual-background prediction through the extrapolation on the next page. The inclusive sample remains an independent cross-check of that prediction.

03Expected limit

Expected 90% CL limits

Background-only expectation using and asymptotic profile likelihood.

Background-shape uncertainties are uncorrelated between bins in the reported construction.

arXiv:2609.05900
notes:
At each mass, we sum the contributions from all 3 production mechanisms in every region. A common signal-strength parameter scales them because their rates depend on the same kinetic mixing. We use a binned profile likelihood with nuisance parameters to obtain expected 90% CL (Confidence Level) limits using CLs (the modified frequentist confidence-level method) under the background-only hypothesis. The reported construction treats shape uncertainties as uncorrelated between bins and uses a Poisson prescription for background normalisation. The regions do not share events, although detector uncertainties can be correlated between them.

title: Positron study: results and refinements
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Positron study: results and refinements
Completed analysis

Accomplished in this study

  • Detector-level efficiencies for three production mechanisms
  • Three exclusive regions and all channel-to-region migrations
  • Dedicated background predictions and an inclusive cross-check
  • Combined 90% CL sensitivity at the 8 GeV benchmark
Further refinements

Opportunities to improve

  • Detector-response inputs informed by measurements
  • Efficient sampling of rare background tails
  • Extended uncertainty models for new configurations
notes:
The positron analysis is complete for the 8 GeV Baseline 1 benchmark. We evaluated each production mechanism in every reconstructed category, included migration, obtained the background predictions and combined the three exclusive regions. The result demonstrates the sensitivity gain from annihilation, especially near 90 MeV.

Further studies can refine the detector-response inputs using measurements, increase the statistics available for rare-background studies, and extend the uncertainty models as new detector and beam configurations are explored. These are directions for developing the analysis beyond the completed benchmark.

title: Main results
body:
Summary and outlook
# Main results
My software contributions

Framework design and implementation

  • General framework design; simulation software (DSimu) and event model (DEvent)
  • Rare-process biasing, staged filtering and production optimisation
  • ACTS integration for tracking and ECAL extrapolation
Positron-beam analysis

Combined positron sensitivity

Three production mechanisms, full detector simulation and three exclusive signal regions, including all channel-to-region migrations.

90% CL expected limit at 90 MeV
POT, 8 GeV, Baseline 1

Annihilation improves the projected reach near 90 MeV by about two orders of magnitude.
notes:
My software contributions cover the general framework design, the development of DSimu and DEvent, rare-process biasing and filtering, production optimisation, and ACTS integration. Together with the collaboration's response and reconstruction work, these components connect simulated interactions to the observables used in the physics analysis.

I used this framework to complete a detector-level positron-beam study with three production mechanisms and three exclusive signal regions. The signal calculation includes migration between all channel and region combinations. Combining the regions gives an expected 90 percent confidence-level limit of 5.33 times ten to the minus thirteen in epsilon squared at a mediator mass of 90 MeV and three times ten to the fourteen POT. At the same detector benchmark and matching integrated luminosity, annihilation improves the reach near this mass by about two orders of magnitude relative to the earlier electron-beam projection.

title: Outlook
body:
Summary and outlook
# Outlook
Detector response

Tune digitisation, calibration and veto selections with prototype and beam-test measurements.

Rare-process simulation

Increase dedicated background statistics with improved sampling and more detailed uncertainty models.

Positron beam energies

Extend the analysis to additional design energies and optimise selections for each mass range.

Changing the positron beam energy shifts the annihilation mass range.
notes:
The completed framework and 8 GeV study support several extensions. Prototype and beam-test measurements can provide more detailed response inputs for digitisation, calibration and veto optimisation. Improved rare-process sampling can increase the statistics available for background studies and support more detailed uncertainty models.

A further physics direction is to vary the positron design energy. The characteristic annihilation mass scales approximately as the square root of the beam energy. Studies at additional energies can therefore explore other mediator masses, with selections optimised for the corresponding recoil and photon kinematics. This extends the physics coverage beyond the 8 GeV benchmark.
